explanation: SET NOCOUNT is explicitly set to OFF, causing row-count messages to be returned to the client, increasing network overhead.
SET XACT_ABORT is explicitly set to OFF, allowing some runtime errors to leave a transaction partially applied.
SELECT * couples callers to every current and future column of Sales.Orders, risking breakage on schema changes.
SELECT TOP (10) returns an arbitrary set of rows because no ordering is specified.
DISTINCT is used where OrderID is already the primary key, adding redundant sort/dedup overhead.
WITH (NOLOCK) can return uncommitted, missing, or duplicated rows, violating data consistency.
YEAR() applied directly to OrderDate prevents index seeks, forcing a table/index scan.
Comparing int CustomerID with nvarchar @CustomerIdText forces implicit conversion, defeating index usage.
OR-based optional filtering prevents efficient seeking and breaks cardinality estimation.
LIKE '%urgent%' uses a leading wildcard, preventing index seeks and forcing full scans.
NOT IN returns no rows when the subquery contains any NULL, causing incorrect filtering results.
ISNULL() on CustomerID in a predicate prevents index usage by evaluating per row.
Adding 0 to OrderID forces arithmetic evaluation per row, preventing direct index matching.
Inequality (<>) on CustomerID often forces broad table scans instead of targeted seeks.
Cross joining Orders and Customers without filtering multiplies rows and wastes resources.
Comma-separated tables in FROM with predicates in WHERE obscure join logic and risk accidental cartesian products.
Scalar subquery executes per outer row, degrading performance versus a set-based join.
Correlated EXISTS check runs per outer row; a set join would be more efficient.
The CASE expression is duplicated in SELECT and ORDER BY, increasing parsing and execution overhead.
ORDER BY 2 references a column position, making the query fragile to select list changes.
OFFSET/FETCH without a unique tie-breaker produces inconsistent page contents across runs.
UNION performs unnecessary duplicate elimination between already disjoint literal branches.
COUNT(*) > 0 calculates full row counts when a simple EXISTS check suffices.
SELECT @var = column silently accepts multiple rows and keeps the last value, causing unpredictable results.
Table variables often receive inaccurate cardinality estimates on older compatibility levels, leading to poor plans.
SELECT ... INTO creates temp tables implicitly, making schema maintenance and indexing difficult.
CURSOR processing executes row-by-row, bypassing SQL Server's set-based optimization engine.
WHILE loops processing rows iteratively defeat set-based operations and increase execution time.
Concatenating variable values directly into SQL text enables SQL injection and prevents plan caching.
Using sp_executesql but embedding values instead of parameterizing them defeats plan reuse and security.
Temp table #Scratch is created but never dropped, persisting until procedure scope ends and risking collisions.
CATCH block logs the error but neither rethrows it nor signals failure, masking issues from callers.
RAISERROR is deprecated for new error paths; THROW preserves execution context and error details.
PRINT output is buffered and unsuitable for structured diagnostics or automated logging pipelines.
Embedding business identifier 1 directly in the query violates parameterization and portability standards.
Unlabelled date constant '20160101' lacks context, making the query difficult to maintain.
String '01/02/2016' converted without an explicit style parameter depends on session settings, causing misinterpretation.
COALESCE in join predicate prevents normal index usage and forces full scans on both sides.
Self-joining Orders to retrieve the same key adds unnecessary processing without returning new data.
Sorting by Comments (max text) forces expensive wide sorts, impacting memory grants and performance.
Aggregating the entire OrderLines fact table without filters wastes CPU and I/O on large datasets.
Row-level predicate placed in HAVING instead of WHERE executes grouping before filtering unnecessarily.
ORDER BY on an aggregate returning one row forces an unnecessary sort operation.
MERGE has documented concurrency and correctness edge cases; separate IF/UPDATE/INSERT blocks are safer.
Setting Comments to itself triggers logging and locking without changing data, wasting resources.
Deleting on Quantity = -1 is a broad business value check, risking accidental deletion of valid historical data.
WAITFOR DELAY blocks a worker thread, reducing concurrency and should be handled asynchronously.
Transaction begins outside a TRY/CATCH block, risking orphaned transactions on runtime errors.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT changes session state, introducing fragile coupling and potential constraint violations.
Calling sp_who without schema qualification forces SQL Server to search sysdb and msdb, degrading performance.
Changing ROWCOUNT and not resetting it affects all subsequent queries in the session unpredictably.
INSERT INTO without explicit column names fails on schema changes and relies on table definition order.
Concatenating @CustomerName directly into dynamic SQL text creates a direct SQL injection vector.
UPDATE lacks a WHERE clause, modifying every row in #DemoCustomers and causing unintended data loss.
Predicate on Sales.Orders placed in WHERE converts the LEFT JOIN to an INNER JOIN, filtering out non-matching customers.
Comparing DeliveryMethodID to NULL with = always evaluates to UNKNOWN; use IS NULL instead.
Scalar UDF GetCustomerType evaluates row-by-row, disabling parallelism and killing performance on large sets.
CATCH block inside a transaction does not roll back, risking committed partial work or orphaned transactions.
Explicit index hint WITH (INDEX = 1) forces a specific execution plan, reducing adaptability to data changes.
Four levels of nested subqueries are difficult to read and maintain; refactor to CTEs or temp tables.
SELECT * against a multi-value function couples the caller to internal column definitions and wastes bandwidth.
